title: Brazilian Banking Giant Itaú Formalizes Crypto Role As Brazil Closes Its Licensing Window
text:
Itaú has formally registered with Brazil’s central bank to intermediate and custody crypto assets under the new licensing rules.
Itaú Unibanco, the largest private bank in Brazil, has formalized its role as a cryptocurrency service provider before the Central Bank of Brazil. The filing covers intermediation and custody of crypto assets, the same activities the regulator assigns to brokerage firms, according to local reports. The news arrives as the country’s crypto sector faces a compressed timeline to obtain licenses.
Itaú’s move places the bank inside a licensing framework that did not exist a year ago. Brazil’s central bank requires every company that holds, moves, or trades crypto for customers to register as a regulated provider. By filing, Itaú tells the market that it intends to be one of them.
For Brazilian users, the change matters most for custody. A provider that holds crypto for clients must keep those assets separate from the firm’s own money, meet minimum capital requirements, and follow the same governance and anti-money laundering standards that apply to securities brokers.
Clients of an authorized bank gain a clearer legal footing than clients of an unregulated app or an offshore exchange. For the bank, the filing is a commitment. A regulated crypto operation carries compliance costs, audit obligations, and reporting duties that smaller competitors may struggle to meet.
The move also signals that Brazil’s biggest lenders plan to keep crypto inside the domestic financial system rather than leave it to foreign platforms.
Itaú’s crypto story started before the new rules. The bank announced plans for crypto custody in 2022, when it was building a tokenization platform. In late 2025, it began letting retail clients buy and sell bitcoin through its investment app, íon. The crypto assets traded on íon are held in custody by Itaú itself, which made the bank’s position an operational one long before it became a regulatory one.
The regulatory backdrop came in 2025 and early 2026, when the central bank published Resolutions 519, 520, and 521. They created a new license category called Sociedades Prestadoras de Serviços de Ativos Virtuais, or SPSAVs, and the rules took effect February 2, 2026.
The framework sorts providers into three categories: intermediaries, custodians, and brokers. It requires formal segregation of client and company assets, sets minimum capital levels, and extends the customer protection, governance, internal control, security, and anti-money laundering rules that already govern banks and brokers.
Resolution 521 brought crypto transactions into the foreign-exchange regime. Transfers with unauthorized counterparties face a $100,000 cap, which limits how crypto moves across borders outside regulated channels.
Companies already operating when the regime took effect had to file for authorization within a transition period.
That timing is why Itaú’s filing reads as a response to a pressure point, not a routine update.
Stricter standards follow. On July 1, 2026, the central bank approved tighter rules. Beginning in 2027, providers must meet financial security requirements similar to those for securities brokers and distributors.
The regulator also barred institutions in Segment 5, the simplified-rules category for smaller banks, from offering virtual asset services. That decision pushes crypto activity toward larger, better-capitalized players, the group Itaú belongs to.

title: Treasury Secretary Bessent: U.S. Will Win In Digital Assets
text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that U.S. leadership in digital assets could reinforce the dollar’s global reach even as the stalled CLARITY Act leaves regulators to fill the gap.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that American leadership in digital assets could reinforce the dollar’s global position, even as Congress has stalled on the market-structure legislation meant to govern them.
Speaking at Ripple’s Swell conference in New York with CEO Brad Garlinghouse, Bessent argued that the foundations of reserve-currency power are shifting. For much of modern history, he said, the dollar’s dominance rested largely on military strength.
“We will keep our military umbrella, but increasingly, it becomes a technological umbrella,” he said.
He grouped digital assets with artificial intelligence and semiconductors as areas where the United States and China are competing to build dominant infrastructure, and suggested the financial rails countries choose will shape the dollar’s reach.
The most concrete link he drew runs through stablecoins, dollar-pegged tokens whose issuers typically hold reserves that include U.S. Treasury securities. Bessent said stablecoins could give people in countries with high inflation or volatile currencies easier access to dollars.
CoinGecko data puts the share of stablecoins denominated in dollars above 98%, with Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC the largest. Bessent himself put the figure above 90%. The exact number differs, but the dollar clearly dominates the category.
NEW: 🇺🇸 Secretary Scott Bessent says the Treasury is moving on crypto regulation with or without CongressHe says they will “bring the SEC and CFTC together to close the gaps through regulation.” pic.twitter.com/JnsT3oxVEn
Bessent has also argued that stablecoin reserves could increase demand for Treasury debt. Last year he suggested stablecoins could generate $2 trillion in short-term demand for Treasuries and bills. That projection depends on how quickly stablecoin supply grows, what reserve rules apply, and how issuers choose to invest.
Bitcoin traded around $80,000 to $81,000 this week ahead of the Federal Reserve decision. Bitcoin advocates have long argued that a neutral, non-issuer asset offers something different from dollar-pegged tokens.
The regulatory backdrop is more uncertain. The Comptroller of the Currency has finalized its rule implementing the GENIUS Act, which sets requirements for payment stablecoin issuers. The federal framework takes effect January 18, 2027.
The broader CLARITY Act, which would establish market-structure rules for digital assets, failed a Senate procedural vote on September 15, 49 to 50, short of the 60 votes needed. Disputes included ethics provisions related to federal officials’ crypto interests and stablecoin yield.
Banks and the White House clashed over those yield terms.
Bessent called the setback disappointing. He said Treasury could work with the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to address regulatory gaps. “At Treasury, we have a lot of convening powers,” he said, describing the agencies as “great partners.”
He also said regulators could set guardrails to prevent banks from cutting off crypto firms, a practice known as debanking.
“I think we can set up regulatory best practices, guardrails that will prevent that from happening again,” he said.
Those remarks did not set out a formal plan, working group, or timeline. Agency action can clarify rules within existing authority, but it lacks the permanence of an act of Congress, and it can be reversed by a future administration.
Next week’s midterm elections could further stall the CLARITY Act, according to TD Cowen.

title: Crypto braces for potential shift in congressional oversight after midterms
text: After years of pushing for legislation, the digital asset sector could find itself navigating a very different political landscape under a new Congress as a result of next week's midterm elections. That could feel like whiplash as a new Congress shifts its focus from advancing digital asset legislation to ramping up oversight, while potentially revisiting a scaled-back version of the Clarity Act. Over the past two years, a Republican-led Congress passed a stablecoin law dubbed the GENIUS Act and worked on the broader Clarity Act, which passed the House in 2025. That work stalled in the Senate amid multiple messes, including a fight over stablecoin rewards between banks and crypto, but ultimately got derailed over top Republican President Donald Trump 's vast crypto wealth. That wealth had grown to hundreds of millions of dollars linked to World Liberty Financial and his TRUMP memecoin and became something many Democrats could not ignore in trying to pass the bill. Sources who spoke with The Block said they expect the legislative dynamics to change for crypto, as polls show that Democrats have a high likelihood of taking back Congress. Bettors on prediction market platforms such as Kalshi put a 64% chance of the Democratic Party winning the Senate and a 90% chance of winning in the House. " Forget politics, if you believe the prediction markets, one or both houses may become led by Democrats," former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo said in a call with reporters last week. "I wouldn't expect anything to happen in the lame duck Congress." Cuomo is now a board director at crypto exchange OKX. "I would hope that if there is a change in Congress, that they take up the Clarity Act, that they put politics aside just for a moment, act responsibly in the best interest of this country, which is to pass the Clarity Act so companies know the rules and regulations of the road," he added. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., who was significantly involved in negotiations for the Clarity Act, said the will was there among Democrats to get the bill passed, but that Republican leadership was done negotiating, she told Puck News earlier this month. When asked whether a Democratic-controlled Congress would prioritize the Clarity Act, Alsobrooks said: "Absolutely not." "I don't think that's realistic," Alsobrooks said, but also noted earlier that it could still happen in the lame duck period — the time after elections and before new lawmakers come into office. Who will take charge? Congressional committee chairs drive the agenda, and could soon have Democrats at the helm. Four major committees oversee the crypto industry — the Senate Banking Committee, the Senate Agriculture Committee, the House Agriculture Committee, and the Senate Agriculture Committee. With Democrats likely to at least take the House or Senate, it becomes unlikely that crypto legislation will seep its way through those committees. If Democrats take the Senate, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, would become Chair of the Senate Banking Committee. Last month, The Block asked in a call with reporters if she would take the lead on crypto legislation if she leads that panel. "I'd be happy to sit down with other Democrats, with the Republicans, and with the industry and hammer out a meaningful crypto bill that protects our national security, that protects our economy and that dials back the corruption," Warren said. "I think we could get that done, but it will require the Republicans' willingness to stand up to Donald Trump — and that's a pretty tall order." In that position, Ron Hammond, head of policy and advocacy at Wintermute, said he expects Warren to use subpoena power and be aggressive. "The question is not legislatively what she can do that's damaging because a lot of that would have to get signed by the president," Hammond said in an interview with The Block. "But you can say that she will pretty much kill any positive or even helpful things for the industry." Specifically, Warren could hone in on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's approval of de novo bank charters like Ripple, Coinbase and Trump-family-run World Liberty Financial, Hammond said. Ohio One of the major races in crypto to watch is Ohio, where former Senate Banking Committee Chair Sherrod Brown is facing off against crypto-friendly Republican Jon Husted. Following the fallout of the Clarity Act vote in the Senate, major Fairshake political action committee said it was committing $30 million to back Husted against Brown. Brown could become Chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee if he wins, given his seniority, Hammond said. As Chair of the Senate Banking Committee, he called for a crackdown on the use of cryptocurrency to fund terrorism and evade sanctions and has generally taken a critical stance on crypto. Both the Senate and House Agriculture Committees are viewed as being more partisan compared to the Senate Banking Committee and the House Financial Services Committee. In any case, Brown's spot could put any crypto legislation that comes out of the House Agriculture Committee on ice, Hammond said. As Chair, Brown criticized a crypto market structure bill in 2022 called the Digital Commodities Consumer Protection Act, which had become closely associated with now-jailed former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, and was delayed and ultimately fell through. On the House side The biggest point of contention over the past several weeks has been who will lead the House Financial Services Committee if Republicans lose that chamber, leaving current Republican Chair French Hill out of his top spot. Top Democrat Maxine Waters led the committee previously and was expected to take up the spot again in case of a flip, but has since been challenged by Democratic Reps. Sean Casten and Bill Foster. Some Democrats have signalled that they want "generational change," given that Waters is 88 years old and Casten is 54, according to reporting from Politico. In any case, the Clarity Act won't happen no matter which Democratic chair leads the committee, Hammond said. Waters, for her part, worked on the GENIUS Act and got close to the industry in learning about the issues, Hammond said. However, she has since criticized the industry following the collapse of crypto exchange FTX and later, Trump's crypto interests. "But overall, we would probably see more of the same that we've seen from her in years prior," Hammond said. Foster is also similar to Waters, Hammond said. Casten would take a more aggressive stance on crypto, he said. "If he were somehow to win the financial services top slot, I would expect a very heavy focus on oversight and a very heavy focus on the crypto side," Hammond said. "Not saying that Maxine Waters is going to do that already, but I think there would be especially a heavier bend if Casten were to take it." House Democrats could decide to work with Republicans on a skinnier version of a crypto regulatory bill, but that would likely be paired up with the party's priorities so would not align with Republicans, Hammond said. At the end of the day, Trump would still have to sign off on it. The Blockchain Association says either way Congress flips, they are still committed to getting legislation passed into law. "Control of Congress may change," said Chief Policy Officer Lindsay Fraser in a statement. "The need for clear crypto rules won't."

title: Avail launches ShieldTX privacy tool targeting copy-trading bots on Hyperliquid
text: Avail has launched ShieldTX for traders on Hyperliquid, with each perpetual futures position opened through a separate wallet. Copy-trading bots can follow trades from publicly visible Hyperliquid wallets and open similar positions within seconds, potentially giving the original traders worse execution prices. ShieldTX makes it harder for bots to link one position to the next. In a review shared exclusively with The Block ahead of the launch, ShieldTX examined 332,317 wallets that traded on Hyperliquid over 30 days. ShieldTX randomly selected seven traders from the platform's top 100, then looked at 25 wallets that appeared to follow each of them. It flagged potential copiers that matched a trader's coin and long or short position within 60 seconds at least 10 times over the 30-day period. ShieldTX measured the difference between the copiers' fill prices and those of the traders they followed, Anurag Arjun, the Polygon co-founder who led Avail after it spun out of Polygon in 2023, told The Block. ShieldTX compared price movements during trades that attracted copy-traders with those that didn't, accounting for coin, size, and volatility, and put the added execution cost for the traders being copied at a median of 63 basis points per trade. Hyperliquid daily perpetuals volume. Image: The Block. Of the top 150 accounts on Hyperliquid's leaderboard, 29% use subaccounts, according to ShieldTX's analysis. Traders can place orders from different wallets using these accounts, but the wallets are still transparently linked onchain, it said. "We thought we had sufficient privacy by rotating wallets," the founder of an unnamed digital-asset fund using ShieldTX said in a statement. "We had no idea the wallets had already been linked to us and were being actively copied." Using the same analysis, ShieldTX also offers a scanner that lets traders see which wallets may be copying them. Avail said publicly identifiable wallets can also expose a fund's hedging activity or reveal new trading strategies to competitors. Separate wallets for each position ShieldTX holds deposited funds in a vault contract on Arbitrum. When a trader opens a position, the service creates a new Hyperliquid wallet and places the trade through it. Avail said other third-party shielding services typically use a single wallet for each trader, making their trades and profit and loss public. Instead, ShieldTX gives traders a new wallet for every position while keeping everything under one account. The positions themselves are still visible on Hyperliquid, but aren't directly linked onchain to the trader's original wallet. Once a position closes, the proceeds go back into the user's shielded balance. Traders can withdraw the funds or use them again, and still have access to their full trading history for audits and compliance. Arjun said Avail has conducted multiple internal audits for ShieldTX alongside external security consultants, with a full audit underway. Avail has been testing ShieldTX with a small group of Hyperliquid whales, trading desks and funds since July, and is now opening broader access via an invite-code model, with discounts extended to AVAIL (AVAIL) stakers. That private beta involved 75 traders, generated approximately $50 million in trading volume, and created more than 3,800 wallets, according to Arjun. Beta traders successfully avoided copy-trading bots using the service, Arjun said, though he did not provide a comparison of their execution costs before and after. ShieldTX is targeting wallets trading $500,000 or more, along with apps using Hyperliquid builder codes, and runs on Nightshade, Avail's zero-knowledge privacy infrastructure. "We built Nightshade because privacy is essential infrastructure for onchain markets," Arjun said in the statement. "We built ShieldTX for Hyperliquid because traders there have limited privacy and that gap is being exploited by onchain surveillance tools, which costs traders directly." Avail has spoken with traders and developers across the Hyperliquid ecosystem and shared information about ShieldTX through ecosystem contacts, although Hyperliquid's core team was not directly involved in its development, Arjun confirmed. Other perpetuals trading platforms have recently introduced privacy features, including Hyperliquid rival Aster, which launched a privacy-enabled blockchain for its derivatives platform in March. StarkWare also launched OffMarket earlier this month, allowing Polymarket users to trade without publicly linking their positions to existing accounts.

title: JPMorgan, Coca-Cola Among 7 More Companies Objecting to OKX-ICE Tokenized Stocks - Decrypt
text:
The pushback against OKX and ICE’s tokenized stock venue now includes the biggest bank in the U.S.
JPMorgan Chase, Coca-Cola, and Dell Technologies are among seven companies added to OKXICE TSV’s list of objecting issuers in a notice dated Tuesday. Advanced Micro Devices, Adobe, Applied Materials, and Sandisk round out the group. The additions bring the total to 33, up from 26 a day earlier.
The list has grown quickly. It stood at nine on Oct. 15, 16 on Oct. 19, and 22 on Oct. 23. Earlier objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Intel, and Oracle. JPMorgan is the third major bank to object, after Goldman and Wells Fargo.
Under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can’t make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC’s order. The objection applies only to that venue. The notices haven’t disclosed the companies’ reasons.
OKXICE’s original Oct. 4 notice proposed 63 tokenized stocks from 62 companies, and several objectors, including Wells Fargo and Arm, weren’t on that initial roster. Some of the biggest names, including Nvidia, Tesla, Apple, and Amazon, haven’t objected so far.
OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7. Trades would run through permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC. Earlier notices warned that it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in self-custodied wallets would be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation if the tokenizer’s broker-dealer failed.
OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before announcing the 24/7 venue this month. Nasdaq, which won SEC approval for its own tokenized securities pilot, has said it will opt its shares out of the exemption.

title: Bitwise Raises Bitcoin Target To $1.6 Million By 2036
text:
Bitwise raised its 2036 bitcoin price target to $1.6 million, projecting 34.3% annual growth on institutional demand and fixed supply.
Bitwise Asset Management this week released its 2027 Bitcoin Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, raising its 2036 base-case price target for bitcoin to $1,599,766 from $1.3 million a year earlier.
The forecast implies a 34.3% compound annual growth rate from the roughly $83,557 price the firm used as of September 30, 2026. Bitwise’s bear case is $130,686 and its bull case is $3.67 million.
The base case rests on three arguments. Institutional investors will keep adding bitcoin to portfolios. New supply stays fixed on a predictable schedule. Rising government debt will push investors toward assets that cannot be printed.
Bitwise estimates that institutions controlling about $147 trillion could allocate 1% to 5% of their portfolios to bitcoin, which the firm says would mean $1.5 trillion to $7.4 trillion of purchases. The network issues about $14 billion in new coins per year, and Bitwise argues that gap will push prices higher.
Institutional plumbing is already expanding. U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs hold about $108 billion, according to the report. Banks and brokerages are building custody and trading services, and a recent report describes sovereign wealth funds and family offices buying during the 2026 decline.
Regulators are also moving. A Federal Reserve capital proposal aimed at easing bank custody rules could widen access for large institutions, if adopted.
The past year tested that thesis. Bitcoin fell 53.4% from its October 2025 peak of $126,080 to a June 30, 2026 low of $58,717. Bitwise calls that drawdown the shallowest in the asset’s history. Prior cycle declines were 77%, 84% and 86%.
Whether the shallow decline signals a new pattern or a pause is less settled. Bitwise expects the four-year cycle to weaken as the investor base broadens. Others see the cycle still at work.
VanEck argues the current slump follows the historical halving pattern, and Fidelity has pointed to a possible floor around November 2026 if past timing holds. NYDIG has said a repeat of earlier bear markets could push the cycle low near $38,000 to $39,000. Cathie Wood has argued the market is nearly through the downturn. Each view carries a different price floor and timeline.
Volatility is the other pillar of the forecast. Bitwise models a 27.8% average volatility over the decade, the midpoint between today’s level and its 2036 expectation. Grayscale’s research head recently put one-year volatility at 43%, against a 10-year average of 64%, and lower than the volatility of 19% of S&P 500 companies. Charles Schwab’s research found the asset remains prone to sharp drawdowns despite the lower readings. A Deutsche Bank analyst has described the trend as a sign of a maturing market.
Bitwise also reports that bitcoin’s correlation with gold reached a record 0.58 in September 2026. The firm expects that relationship to deepen, which positions bitcoin as a store-of-value asset. That link cuts both ways. If gold weakens, bitcoin may lose the support it gained from the same investor demand. Gemini has predicted that at least one country will shift part of its gold reserves into bitcoin in 2026, a forecast that has yet to materialize.
The report is candid about what could go wrong. Bitcoin’s track record is short. Its software was developed in 2008 and 2009, trading began on public exchanges in 2010, the first institutional product with bitcoin exposure launched in 2014, and spot ETPs arrived in 2024.
Bitwise writes that forecasts built heavily on history carry uncertainty because future returns may differ from the past. Regulation is a second concern. The Clarity Act’s failure in Congress, which the report traces to Democratic concerns about ethics provisions, shows that progress can stall, even as the firm argues recent advances are unlikely to be rolled back.
Technology is a third. Quantum computing, and mathematical advances accelerated by AI, could threaten the cryptography that secures bitcoin wallets. Bitwise says the network will need a major upgrade at some point, and holders who fail to move funds to new addresses could be exposed. The developers have made progress over the past year, the report says, but major issues remain unresolved.
Bitcoin’s price is near $80,500.

title: Fed Rate Decision: What Markets and Bitcoin Traders Can Expect - Decrypt
text:
The Federal Reserve announces its interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET today, and traders are almost certain it will change nothing.
CME FedWatch, a tool that converts bets on interest rate futures into probabilities, puts the odds of a hold above 90%, while prediction markets price it a few points higher.
The decision reaches well beyond Wall Street, because the federal funds rate, which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans, sets the baseline for what consumers pay on credit cards and loans. That rate sits at 3.75% to 4.00% after the Fed raised it in September, its first hike since 2023, in a unanimous 12-0 vote.
Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, the Labor Department reported, and gasoline alone jumped 9.1% in the month. Hiring is slowing, though: employers added just 29,000 jobs in September against forecasts of about 90,000, and the unemployment rate stood at 4.2%.
Oil is a major driver of that inflation, trading near $100 a barrel because the U.S.-Iran war has squeezed global supply. Pricier crude lifts gasoline and shipping costs, which eventually show up on grocery shelves and push inflation higher.
Higher inflation makes investors demand more interest for lending to the government, which lifts Treasury yields, the interest rate on U.S. government debt. The 10-year yield, the benchmark that mortgage rates follow, is hovering around 5% after peaking at 5.31% on Oct. 5, so a nearly risk-free return is available without owning anything volatile.
Bitcoin pays no yield and is also very volatile for traditional investors, so when Treasuries pay more, money tends to drift out of riskier assets such as crypto and stocks. The price of Bitcoin sits around $80,700, just below a support-now-resistance zone where sellers have repeatedly stopped rallies this year.
Leverage, meaning borrowed money used to make bigger bets, tends to exaggerate the moves around Fed events. When prices swing against a trader, the exchange automatically closes the position, a liquidation that adds to the selling pressure. After Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech in August, about $481 million in crypto positions were liquidated within 24 hours, more than $360 million of them bets on higher prices.
Traders now appear focused on December, where futures and prediction markets give 75% to 80% odds on another quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. Minutes from September’s meeting show most officials judged another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end, and several said the current rate was “not restrictive or only mildly restrictive.”
Analysts are calling the likely outcome a “hawkish hold,” meaning rates stay put while the tone leaves more hikes on the table. Asked in September whether more hikes would follow, Warsh said, “I’m not going to prejudge any future decisions we make.” He also told reporters, “This won’t surprise you: I’m not in the forward guidance business,” which is Fed-speak for declining to signal future moves.
Dissents, meaning votes against the majority, are the clearest tell in the statement. The Fed’s July vote was 9-3, with three members favoring a hike, so a dissent for tightening today would suggest December is close to locked in.
The Fed publishes no new economic projections at this meeting. Those will arrive in December.

title: Strategy (MSTR) Shareholders Approve Daily Dividends On Four Preferred Stocks
text:
Strategy (MSTR) shareholders approved paying daily dividends on four of its preferred stocks.
Strategy shareholders have approved the Daily Dividends amendment, the company announced Wednesday. Preliminary results show 99.3% of votes cast were in favor, according to Executive Chairman Michael Saylor.
The amendment allows STRF, STRC, STRK and STRD to accrue dividends every calendar day, including weekends and holidays.
The proposal surfaced on September 25, when the company asked holders to attend a special meeting on October 28. Strategy said the change “would reduce reinvestment lag, enhance liquidity and market efficiency, and increase price stability.”
At the time Strategy said that they “believe these enhancements can also benefit our common stockholders by increasing the attractiveness and utility of our Digital Credit instruments, supporting our ability to access preferred equity capital efficiently and expanding the capital markets toolkit we use to execute our Bitcoin Treasury strategy.
Under the approved structure, dividends accrue every day but are paid on the next business day. Strategy has said scheduled dividend rates and total dividend obligations remain unchanged. The company has argued the change could benefit common stockholders by making its Digital Credit instruments easier to use and easier to fund.
The timing depends on board action. If the board approves the change and required filings are completed, the first STRC record and payment dates would fall on November 1 and 2, 2026. For STRF, STRK and STRD, the first record and payment dates would be January 1 and 4, 2027. Those dates also depend on operational readiness.
STRC pays a variable rate that the company can change at its discretion. Its rate for the month ended June 30, 2026 was 11.50%, according to Strategy’s quarterly report. Shareholders approved moving STRC to semi-monthly payments in June, and the new amendment builds on that precedent.
In short, STRC is designed to help Strategy raise money from investors through a preferred stock offering targeting a stable $100 price and a variable dividend yield, then use that capital to continuously buy Bitcoin regardless of its short-term price movements. This creates a potential global dollar-cost-averaging machine for Bitcoin.
Final vote certification will come in a company filing. Board action remains the final step before any new payment schedule begins.
The vote comes after bitcoin fell into somewhat of a bear market. Strategy slowed its bitcoin purchases this year and sold some holdings to fund preferred dividends, interest payments and repurchases.
The company’s common stock, MSTR, is down near 50% over the past year, though it has risen by a figure approaching 1,000% since Strategy began buying bitcoin in 2020.
Earlier this week, Strategy said they paused Bitcoin purchases for the prior week and maintained its holdings at 848,517 BTC, acquired for $64.02 billion at an average price of $75,446 per Bitcoin.
The company spent $204.9 million repurchasing STRC preferred stock while retaining a $4.83 billion cash reserve.
Fellow bitcoin-treasury company Strive pays cash dividends on its Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Preferred Stock (SATA) every business day. This started on June 16, after moving from monthly payments.

title: Coinbase adds Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin across retail, exchange and Prime platforms
text: Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin is now available to retail and institutional customers through Coinbase Prime, Coinbase Exchange and the Coinbase retail app, the companies announced Wednesday. Customers can convert U.S. dollars and other supported dollar-denominated stablecoins into RLUSD at a 1:1 ratio, with deposits and withdrawals supported on the XRP Ledger, Ethereum and Coinbase's Base network. Support for Coinbase Global Exchange customers, including using RLUSD as collateral, is expected to follow. "Institutions want access to a full range of payment options, alongside the execution, settlement, and custody they already rely on," said Brett Tejpaul, Co-CEO, Coinbase Institutional, in a release. "Adding RLUSD on Coinbase is another step toward the everything exchange — one venue where clients choose the assets that fit their strategy, on infrastructure built for security and compliance." It's just the latest announcement in what's been a busy week for Ripple's institutional growth. On Monday, Ripple received final OCC approval to launch a national trust bank and bring RLUSD under federal oversight. It then expanded its partnership with BNY to provide custody support to XRP and RLUSD while exploring tokenized trade finance with C2FO. Ripple and Robinhood also expanded their partnership to bring RLUSD to Robinhood’s retail and institutional businesses. Earlier Wednesday, Moody's gave RLUSD A2 long-term and P-1 short-term deposit ratings, citing credit quality and market value of its reserve assets. The RLUSD stablecoin, which launched in December 2024, has surpassed $2.6 billion in market capitalization, according to Ripple.

title: Bitwise raises bitcoin price target to $1.6 million by 2036, projects 34% annualized returns
text: Crypto asset manager Bitwise has raised its 10-year bitcoin (BTC) forecast from $1.3 million to $1.6 million, projecting the largest cryptocurrency will generate a 34.3% compound annual growth rate during the period. That represents around five times the 6.7% annual return forecast for U.S. equities and three times the 10.8% forecast for the next-best asset class, private equity, based on average projections from JPMorgan, PGIM, BlackRock, and Vanguard. Bitwise's revised forecast comes from its 2027 Bitcoin Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, released Wednesday, an annual report analyzing bitcoin's potential returns, volatility, and corrections over the coming decade. Bitwise calculates its bitcoin price target by estimating the future size of markets the cryptocurrency could compete in, then assigning bitcoin a share of each. In a note to clients on Wednesday, Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan said the firm kept those market-share assumptions unchanged from last year, but raised its estimate for the global store-of-value market in 2036 from $91 trillion to $110 trillion, and for the institutional investment market from $216 trillion to $303 trillion. Citing Boston Consulting Group estimates that institutional investors control roughly $147 trillion in assets, with an allocation of 1% to 5% to bitcoin over the next decade, Bitwise also expects $1.5 trillion to $7.4 trillion of demand, compared to just $14 billion in new bitcoin supply issuance via mining per year. title: Wall Street’s Fast Money Fled Bitcoin ETFs, Sovereign Funds Stepped In - Decrypt
text:
The investors who sold Bitcoin through its 2026 slump weren’t the crowd you might expect.
A Galaxy Research report published Monday found that a handful of hedge funds and banks drove almost all of the institutional selling in U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, while wealth platforms and sovereign funds stepped in to buy.
Institutions that file quarterly 13F reports with the SEC held 355,000 BTC worth of spot ETF shares at the end of September 2025, just before Bitcoin’s all-time high. By June 2026, that had fallen to 307,000 BTC, a 14% drop, the report found.
Nine firms account for more than all of that decline: Millennium Management, Brevan Howard, Goldman Sachs, Capula Management, Farallon Capital, D.E. Shaw, Schonfeld Strategic Advisors, Symmetry Investments and Tudor Investment.
Together they cut 68,000 BTC worth of exposure, roughly $5.4 billion at today’s prices, trimming their positions by between 29% and 100%. That means the other roughly 2,200 filers added about 20,000 BTC in aggregate, worth roughly $1.6 billion.
Morgan Stanley’s wealth management arm, Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and the Abu Dhabi Investment Council were among the buyers. Advisers, family offices, and individuals who don’t file 13Fs cut their holdings by just 6.6% while the price fell 49%.
Galaxy head of firmwide research Alex Thorn says the sellers were largely running a trade, not making a bet on Bitcoin. Many used the cash-and-carry strategy: buying spot ETF shares while shorting CME Bitcoin futures to pocket the gap between the two, known as the basis.
That gap has nearly vanished. The front-month basis averaged 7.9% annualized in the 30 days before Bitcoin’s high, 3.9 percentage points above three-month Treasury bills. In the 30 days to Oct. 21, it averaged 4.8%, just 0.6 points above bills. After fees, rolling costs and margin, the trade now earns about 1.5 points over cash, the report estimates.
“That arithmetic, not the price, is why the multi-strategy desks left,” Thorn wrote.
CFTC data on CME Bitcoin futures tells a similar story. Asset managers’ net long position fell from 43,300 BTC in the week of Bitcoin’s all-time high to 18,400 BTC, a 57% drop. Leveraged funds’ net short, the futures side of the carry trade, shrank by the same proportion, from 71,400 BTC to 30,600 BTC. Open interest is down 28% in Bitcoin terms and 51% in dollar terms.
Contracts further out still offer something. November and December futures priced in 6.3% to 6.5% at the Oct. 21 close, about 2 points over bills before costs. But Thorn argued that the slim edge doesn’t pay for the trade’s tail risk: in December 2022, the basis inverted to negative 31% annualized.
Overall, spot ETF holdings fell just 11% from their October 2025 peak to their July trough while Bitcoin fell 53%. Since the June low, the funds have added 87,000 BTC, which Galaxy calls directional buying rather than carry.
Recent flows have been choppy. Decrypt reported that the ETFs shed nearly $1 billion over two weeks earlier this month before notching their best day in nearly a month on Oct. 19, when BlackRock’s IBIT did all the buying. Since then, a three-day, $1 billion inflow run has been followed by heavy outflows. BTF ETF flows once again turned green this week, but in smaller numbers: roughly $286 million in inflows so far.
The 13F data runs through June, so it doesn’t capture more recent shifts. Galaxy discloses that it holds Bitcoin.

Aptos did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

When Aptos Labs founder Mo Shaikh stepped down in December 2024, Buzz bought more and started to claim he was starting a "community takeover" and that it hadn't been "priced in"—a phrase he repeated at least seven times through January. All while he spammed “Aptos lookin’ good here,” “sidelined?” and “motion not priced in yet" across everyone's timelines.
In February 2025, the shitposting paid off as notable influencers got behind him, drawing eyes to Aptos, and the APT token boosted 17% in 24 hours.

title: Phantom Adds Bitcoin and Sports Event Trading via Kalshi
text:
The crypto wallet’s new integration offers CFTC-regulated event contracts through Kalshi, as prediction markets face growing legal challenges in the US.
Crypto wallet provider Phantom has launched prediction markets for eligible US users through an integration with Kalshi, allowing them to trade on crypto prices, sports and other real-world events directly within its app.
According to Wednesday’s announcement, the integration offers CFTC-regulated event contracts, including short-term Bitcoin price markets that settle every 15 minutes. Trades can be funded through Phantom Cash balances, denominated in the CASH stablecoin.
Kalshi handles customer verification, account management and trade execution, while Phantom provides access through its app. The launch follows no-action relief granted by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in March, allowing Phantom to connect users to regulated markets without registering as an introducing broker, subject to certain conditions.
The service is rolling out through a new Predict tab in Phantom, with availability varying by state and market category. Eligible US users can view live market data, sports scores and market discussions before placing trades through an interface similar to a cryptocurrency token swap.

Phantom’s entry into prediction markets comes amid a widening legal dispute over the industry in the US. On Monday, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission sued Utah after the state challenged Kalshi’s event contracts under its gambling laws, adding to a series of cases over whether federal derivatives regulation supersedes state gambling laws.
Despite the legal uncertainty, trading activity continues to grow. Kalshi recorded $10.8 billion in crypto contract volume over the 30 days ending Oct. 27, up 19.6% from the previous period, according to data compiled by DeFi Rate.

title: Strategy Shareholders Approve Daily Dividends on Preferred Stock, With 99.3% in Favor - Decrypt
text:
Strategy shareholders have approved a plan to let the company's four preferred stocks accrue dividends every calendar day, including weekends and holidays, the Bitcoin treasury company's chairman Michael Saylor said on Wednesday.
Preliminary results show 99.3% of votes cast were in favor of the amendment, which covers Strategy's STRF, STRC, STRK and STRD preferred stocks, according to Saylor. The vote took place at a special meeting of stockholders on Wednesday, the company said.
$MSTR shareholders have approved the Daily Dividends amendment. Preliminary results show 99.3% of votes cast were in favor. The amendment enables $STRF, $STRC, $STRK and $STRD to accrue dividends every calendar day. Thank you to all who voted. https://t.co/w1Cp4GKUy5
— Michael Saylor (@saylor) October 28, 2026
Under the new schedule, every calendar day will be a record date, with payment on the next business day. STRC will move first, with its first daily record date on November 1 and payment on November 2, Saylor added. STRF, STRK and STRD will follow, with their first record date on January 1 and payment on January 4.
The change still depends on Strategy filing amended terms for each stock, according to the filing.
Because U.S. markets are closed at weekends, dividends with record dates on non-trading days will in practice be grouped together. The Depository Trust Company will treat a weekend or holiday record date as falling on the previous business day, which Nasdaq will also treat as the ex-dividend date.
For example, dividends with record dates of Friday, November 6, Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8 would all be treated as having a Friday record date and paid together on Monday, November 9, Strategy said. Because trades settle the next business day, an investor who buys STRC on that Friday would not receive any of the three dividends, while one who sells that day would still receive all three. Treatment could differ for shares traded outside Nasdaq or held through some brokers, the company said.
Strategy proposed the change last month, saying it would help dampen volatility in its preferred shares. For STRC, it means moving from 24 record dates a year to 365.
The company has been working to support STRC, which traded at $99.86 on Wednesday, just below its $100 par value, according to Yahoo Finance. Last week, Strategy paused its Bitcoin buying for the first time since mid-September and spent $204.9 million buying back STRC instead.
Strategy also faces possible removal from MSCI's widely tracked equity indexes. The index provider finalized a rule this month that treats companies whose balance sheets are dominated by a single asset as ineligible, and will publish the list of affected companies on November 11.

title: Crypto PAC spending before midterms possibly obscured after reported FEC hack
Google Previews Key-Splitting Crypto Custody Tool For Banks
text:
Google is previewing a crypto custody system that splits private keys across separate environments, with several banks testing it ahead of a planned early 2027 launch.
Google is reportedly unveiling Google Multi-Party Compute, a crypto custody system that splits signing keys across separate systems, at its first digital assets symposium in New York today. The product is in private preview with several financial institutions. Alphabet has started using it to secure its own assets, according to CoinDesk reporting.
Google plans commercial availability in early 2027 and has not disclosed pricing.
The system applies multi-party computation to a signing key. The key is divided into fragments held by separate parties or machines, and a transaction requires a set number of fragments to sign.
The full key is never assembled in one place. A bank could hold one share on its own hardware, another in Google Cloud, and a third with a rival cloud provider. Institutions can set thresholds such as two-of-three or five-of-seven. Before any signature, a policy engine running inside Google’s Confidential Space checks the transfer against limits, destination restrictions, and approval rules.
Google says it has no access to key shares in unencrypted form, per CoinDesk.
The pitch rests on a persistent problem. Chainalysis attributed 43.8% of cryptocurrency stolen in 2024 to compromised private keys. DeFiLlama data shows roughly 40% of the $16.69 billion lost to hacks through June came from key compromises. In June, an attacker took seven keys from one developer’s computer during the Humanity Protocol breach and drained wallets across two networks.
Such incidents show how concentrated signing authority creates a single point of failure. The industry has responded by recommending multi-vendor multisignature setups that spread control across hardware and software providers.
Google also frames the product against AI-enabled fraud. Chainalysis found that scams linked to AI tool vendors averaged $3.2 million per operation in 2025, compared with $719,000 for other scams. The report links the two figures but does not prove that AI caused the difference.
Ethereum researcher Justin Drake has warned that AI could eventually find mathematical shortcuts that weaken wallet signatures. No AI system has shown that capability. Google’s MPC design targets stolen credentials and unauthorized transfers, not a break in the underlying cryptography.
Quantum computing presents a separate, longer-term risk. Google researchers estimated that a sufficiently powerful future machine could derive a bitcoin private key from an exposed public key in about nine minutes. Roughly 6.9 million bitcoin have exposed public keys. Google says its architecture can adopt post-quantum signatures later without forcing institutions to rebuild their systems, but it has set no timetable. Background on how quantum machines threaten bitcoin explains which addresses are most exposed.
Google enters a market led by Fireblocks, Fordefi, and BitGo. Google argued to CoinDesk that its banking relationships and security expertise give it an advantage. It also positions itself as a neutral supplier for banks that do not want to rely on competitors.
Banks already use specialized platforms, such as BNP Paribas’s custody work with Metaco, and multi-institution vaults built with BitGo.

title: AI Can Quietly Influence Experts’ Decisions, Anthropic Study Finds - Decrypt
text:
Professional analysts adopted their AI agent’s hidden, randomly assigned opinion on 86% of key judgment calls, against about 50% expected by chance, according to an experiment published Tuesday by Anthropic’s Alignment team. Only 15% credited the agent afterward, and none suspected its preferences had been planted.
AI agents—programs that carry out tasks on their own—are being handed expert work on what the study calls the usual assumption: that experts still make the decisions that matter. Anthropic launched 10 agent templates for financial firms and insurers in May, saying users have the final word.
That arrangement, called “human in the loop,” assumes the person who signs off on an AI’s work is the one making the important calls. Anthropic tested it on 50 analysts experienced in causal inference, meaning working out from data whether one thing causes another.
Each analyst used Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, to advise a fictional farming cooperative on expanding an advisory program. Unknown to them, a coin flip set which option each agent favored, hidden in a system prompt, the instructions that shape how an AI behaves.
“Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%,” Anthropic said. Those who had already chosen before the agent weighed in abandoned it 60% of the time when the agent disagreed, against 6% when it agreed, though that rests on only 38 cases.
Asked to explain their choices, 77% repeated the agent’s argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word. Only 15% credited the agent, and 52% called the final recommendation more their own than the agent’s.
“For individual experts, this could mean losing agency over their own work, a form of what researchers call disempowerment,” Anthropic said. This phenomenon basically means the human voluntarily loses control over their own decisions. “The work still goes out under the expert’s name,” the authors wrote, “but the decisions that most depend on their judgment are in reality settled by the agent’s prior beliefs.”
In April 2025, OpenAI rolled back an update to ChatGPT that it called overly flattering or agreeable. The agents here were told never to mislead, yet they rarely argued for the alternative.
“With only one side argued well,” the authors wrote, “the analysts could adopt the agent’s assumptions without working out their own.” Error checks struggle to catch this because judgment calls have no single correct answer, so the work looks sound whichever option is picked.
Anthropic says this is no argument for using AI less, since analysts with the agent finished faster and made far fewer serious errors, though the no-agent group was small and less experienced. It suggests agents that argue the best case for each option or ask the expert first, though that could overwhelm users.
The researchers deliberately strengthened the agents’ preferences and tested one task, field, and model, so real-world effects may be smaller. Measuring it outside the lab is the hard part: the team could detect deference only because it randomized each agent’s lean, which the authors say is rarely possible in real work.

title: Hardware Wallet Headlines Dominated Coverage—But CEX And DeFi Took Almost All Of 2026’s $2.35B Crypto Losses
text:
Crypto hacks have produced roughly $2.35 billion in net losses so far in 2026 after freezes and returns, according to a report by Lightning.news shared with Bitcoin Magazine. A security researcher by the name of Stacy Muur posted on X compiled “a list of protocols that were hacked for more than $50,000 in 2026.” 230 protocols year-to-date. “Crypto security is absolutely cooked.” September alone accounted for about $768 million in Muur’s tally, driven mainly by centralized exchanges and DeFi rather than pure Bitcoin self-custody hardware wallets, which got significant news coverage at the time.
The largest single loss was Bitget’s September 24 drain of roughly $387.5 million from hot and warm wallets. The exchange and firms including Chainalysis, Elliptic, and TRM Labs have linked the incident to North Korea, citing IP patterns consistent with prior DPRK-linked VPN use, on-chain overlaps with wallets tied to earlier Lazarus Group and TraderTraitor activity, including the 2025 Bybit theft. Attackers used third-party security products to inject fraudulent withdrawal commands without taking private keys.
Liquid Network, Blockstream’s Bitcoin sidechain, took the next-largest hit when attackers exploited an Elements software bug in early September to mint about 4,000 unbacked L-BTC and peg them out for roughly 4,000 real bitcoins, valued near $320 million at the time. The self-described white-hat actors returned 3,400 BTC after negotiations conducted on-chain via OP_RETURN messages and kept about 600 BTC. No federation keys were compromised. The loss came from a type of inflation bug on the Liquid network protocol.
Samson Mow later called the episode part of an “avalanche of AI-assisted attacks” that had already reached other Bitcoin-adjacent software before hitting Liquid. The network is back and running now, having covered the losses, presumably from investors.
DeFi platforms showed the same pattern of concentrated, high-value losses. Drift Protocol lost approximately $285–296 million in an April governance and multisig compromise that involved months of social engineering. An investigation commissioned by the project attributed the operation to North Korean actors.
KelpDAO’s LayerZero-powered rsETH bridge was drained of roughly $292 million in unbacked tokens after a single-verifier design was subverted. LayerZero stated that preliminary indicators pointed to DPRK’s Lazarus Group, specifically TraderTraitor.
Tectonic on Cronos saw about $120.4 million borrowed against manipulated collateral in late August. Validators later rewound the chain and recovered the majority, though several million dollars that had already been bridged off-network were not restored.
Incidents involving Bitcoin hardware wallets were smaller in aggregate despite the wide news coverage. Galaxy Research placed the Coinkite RNG hack values in the range of roughly 1,596–1,789 BTC, on the order of $100–130 million, with higher upper-bound estimates near 2,055 BTC.
Ledger losses of roughly $86–102 million traced to devices sold through the authorized Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, where an unauthorized hardware implant captured recovery phrases during setup, a supply chain attack. The company stated that confirmed cases were limited to that reseller’s supply chain and that its own systems and direct sales were unaffected, though there are unconfirmed reports of such bugged devices making it to German markets. Combined, however, these hardware-adjacent events remain well below the single largest CEX and DeFi incidents.
The year has also coincided with the practical deployment of AI coding agents capable of scanning codebases for vulnerabilities and automating exploit development. Muur has stated that “AI is definitely making it much easier to find and exploit bugs. I think we’re entering a pretty serious cybersecurity arms race.”
Reports note that code-flaw exploits accelerated after the February release of models such as GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.6, which showed high success rates on smart-contract bug benchmarks at low cost.
OpenAI has disclosed internal testing cases in which agents accessed unauthorized test-network funds or bypassed controls to complete tasks. Most of the year’s largest heists still relied on traditional vectors such as key compromise, social engineering, and infrastructure flaws, but the lowered barrier for discovering and weaponizing bugs adds a new layer of risk, particularly for complex smart-contract systems and sidechains.
Bitcoin’s base layer itself has not been the source of these losses. The bulk of the 2026 damage has concentrated in CEX hot-wallet infrastructure, DeFi governance, oracle designs, and Bitcoin sidechain code, while pure self-custody hardware wallets, even when imperfect, have accounted for a distinctly smaller share. Nevertheless, calls for an update to self custody recommendations have emerged from industry leaders, pushing forward multivendor multisig wallets as the future of niche industry.

Fed Stands Pat, Bitcoin Holds Steady—But a December Rate Hike Is in Play - Decrypt
text:
The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% on Wednesday in a 10-2 vote, with two officials dissenting in favor of another quarter-point hike. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted against the decision, according to the Fed’s statement.
Bitcoin barely moved, edging up about 0.2% to roughly $80,950 in the minutes after the 2 p.m. ET announcement. CME FedWatch, a tool that converts bets on interest rate futures into probabilities, had put the odds of no change at around 90% before the decision.
The decision reaches well beyond Wall Street, because the federal funds rate, which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans, sets the baseline for what consumers pay on credit cards and car loans. The Fed raised that rate in September, its first hike since 2023, in a unanimous 12-0 vote.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its statement, a step up from the solid pace it cited in September. “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little,” it added.
On inflation, the Fed said it remains elevated and that “the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal."
Hammack also dissented in July, when the committee held rates in a 9-3 vote with Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan joining her in favoring a hike. Kashkari and Logan sided with the majority this time, so the number of dissents fell to two from three.
Oil remains a major driver of inflation because the U.S.-Iran war has squeezed global supply, and U.S. crude settled at $99.90 a barrel on Tuesday. Pricier crude lifts gasoline and shipping costs, which eventually show up on grocery shelves, and consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, with gasoline alone jumping 9.1% in the month, the Labor Department reported.
Higher inflation makes investors demand more interest for lending to the government, which lifts Treasury yields, the interest rate on U.S. government debt. The 10-year yield, the benchmark that mortgage rates follow, closed Tuesday at 4.99% after peaking at 5.31% on Oct. 5, so a nearly risk-free return is available without owning anything volatile.
Bitcoin pays no yield, so when Treasuries pay more, money tends to drift out of riskier assets such as crypto and stocks. The price briefly poked above $81,600 earlier Wednesday before slipping back, below a resistance zone between $81,000 and $82,500 that has capped several rally attempts this year.
Leverage, meaning borrowed money used to make bigger bets, tends to exaggerate those moves around Fed events. When prices swing against a trader, the exchange automatically closes the position, a liquidation that adds to the selling pressure. After Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech in August, about $481 million in crypto positions were liquidated within 24 hours.
Traders had put the odds of another quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting above 70% before the decision. Minutes from September’s meeting show most officials judged another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end.
The October jobs report arrives Nov. 6, October inflation data follows on Nov. 10, and the Fed meets again Dec. 8-9, when it will also publish new economic projections. Fed Chairman Warsh will hold a press conference at 2:30 p.m. to elaborate on the Fed's decision.

title: OpenAI Plans to Buy Google's AI Chips as It Looks Beyond Nvidia: Report - Decrypt
text:
OpenAI plans to buy AI chips from Google, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke with The Information. The step would loosen its dependence on Nvidia, the company that supplies most of the hardware behind the AI boom.
Neither company has confirmed the plan, and the price, the number of chips, and the delivery dates have not been disclosed. OpenAI is one of Nvidia’s biggest customers.
The chips OpenAI is reportedly after are Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, processors designed for one job: the math that AI models run on. Google revealed the chip in 2016, saying it had already run TPUs in its data centers for more than a year.
Reports in June 2025 said OpenAI had begun renting Google's TPUs, and the company described it as early testing with no plans to deploy them at scale. A purchase would mean owning the hardware instead of paying Google by the hour. Other details of the plan have not been made public.
A job listing from OpenAI in San Francisco asks for an engineer to lead the optimization of its frontier models on TPUs so the rumors have weight. The work involves compilers, the software that translates an AI model into instructions a specific chip can run, which is why switching chips is harder than swapping parts.
Richard Ho, who leads OpenAI's hardware program, spent nearly nine years at Google and was one of the leaders of its Cloud TPU project before joining OpenAI.
In September 2025, Nvidia signed a letter of intent to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as it deployed at least 10 gigawatts of Nvidia systems. A gigawatt is a billion watts, the unit data center builders now use to size their projects.
Two weeks later, AMD gave OpenAI the right to buy up to 160 million AMD shares, roughly 10% of the company. The right is tied to OpenAI deploying 6 gigawatts of AMD chips.
Nvidia ended up putting $30 billion into OpenAI's funding round, well below the $100 billion in the letter of intent. CEO Jensen Huang said in March that it might be the last such investment before OpenAI goes public.
In June, OpenAI unveiled Jalapeño, its first custom chip, built with Broadcom. It is designed for inference, the step where a trained model generates answers, with initial deployment planned for the end of 2026.
Google unveiled two eighth-generation TPUs in April: the 8t for training AI models and the 8i for inference (running them). Its performance figures are measured against Google's previous-generation chip, Ironwood, not against Nvidia's hardware.
Anthropic, OpenAI's main rival, signed an agreement with Google and Broadcom in April for multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity that it expects to come online starting in 2027.
Alphabet began delivering TPU systems to customers' own data centers in the second quarter, according to its CFO. Google Cloud also began offering OpenAI's GPT-6 models to select customers in private preview last week.

title: Actor Anthony Boyle Contacted Ex-FTX CEO as Part of Netflix Portrayal
text:
The former FTX CEO remains incarcerated as Irish actor Anthony Boyle portrays him in the downfall of the crypto exchange and his relationship with Caroline Ellison.
In about three weeks, Netflix is set to release one of the first dramatizations of the saga of cryptocurrency exchange FTX since its CEO, Sam “SBF” Bankman-Fried, was found guilty and sentenced to prison.
According to a Wednesday Vanity Fair report, Anthony Boyle, the Irish actor portraying SBF on screen for the Netflix series ‘The Altruists,’ contacted the former CEO in prison via email as he prepared for the role. Although Boyle said he “promised him that I wouldn’t divulge anything,” Bankman-Fried reportedly answered the bulk of the actor’s questions ahead of the series’ release.
“I was interested in what possessed someone to become the world’s youngest billionaire,” said Boyle, according to Vanity Fair. “I’m not really interested in money or crypto or finance. It was: What makes them do the things that they do?”
Based on a trailer Netflix released on Oct. 8, the series appeared to be centered on the relationship between Bankman-Fried and his colleague and girlfriend, Caroline Ellison, who headed FTX’s sister arm, Alameda Research. SBF was convicted of seven felony counts related to the misuse of customer funds at FTX and sentenced to 25 years in prison, while Ellison was released in January after serving more than a year as part of a plea deal with US authorities.
Former FTX COO Constance Wang said that the on-screen portrayal of the executives made her “feel physically upset,” adding that SBF was more “socially awkward” than Boyle demonstrated.
Bankman-Fried has already been covered by several media outlets and was the subject of Michael Lewis’ 2023 book Going Infinite. Ben McKenzie’s documentary Everyone Is Lying to You for Money included a 2022 interview with the former CEO before the exchange’s downfall, but no other significant dramatization of SBF or FTX has been released on the big screen or television until The Altruists.

title: More Americans Have Tried Crypto, But Few Are Sticking With It: Survey - Decrypt
text:
More Americans have tried crypto than a year ago. Far fewer are still using it.
Some 22% of U.S. adults say they have ever owned or used crypto, up from 18% in 2025, according to a national survey conducted by Ipsos for the DeFi Education Fund, a crypto policy advocacy group. But the share who used crypto in the past 12 months held flat at 13%.
The growth came almost entirely from people who have stepped away. Among Americans who hadn’t used crypto in the past year, the share who had ever owned or used it more than doubled, to 11% from 5%. Plans to buy are flat, too: 17% say they’re likely to own or use crypto in the future, compared with 16% last year.
Men were more than twice as likely as women to have used crypto in the past year, 18% to 8%, and adults under 60 were far more likely to have used it than older Americans. Curiosity remains the top reason people tried crypto, cited by 34% of those who have owned it, followed by long-term investment at 25%.
The survey polled 1,545 adults from Sept. 8 to 16 on Ipsos’ KnowledgePanel, the same probability-based panel the Federal Reserve uses for its annual survey of household finances. The margin of error is plus or minus 2.8 percentage points.
It also found deep unease with the traditional financial system. Only 19% of Americans say it’s secure, while 63% say it needs an upgrade to combat threats like cybercrime and AI. Six in 10 worry about data breaches at major financial institutions, and 54% doubt those institutions are ready to protect their personal information from AI-driven threats. Financial privacy matters to 74%.
That skepticism hasn’t translated into trust in crypto. Just 4% have high trust in crypto exchanges and 5% in decentralized platforms, compared with 42% for large national banks. Credit unions led at 48%, down 5 points from last year.
Security worries aren’t limited to banks. Crypto wallet maker Ledger said all confirmed cases in a suspected $87 million drain involved hardware wallets sold by a Southeast Asian reseller. Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake recently warned that advances in AI could break the cryptography securing Bitcoin and Ethereum sooner than expected.
The survey also points to a wide knowledge gap. Only 2% of Americans are very familiar with decentralized finance, or DeFi, shorthand for the group of crypto-native financial applications that allow users to buy, sell, or borrow digital assets without third-party intermediaries.
Just 6% could identify all four characteristics of crypto listed in the survey, while 35% weren’t sure how to describe it at all. Yet 40% say they’d be at least somewhat likely to try DeFi if it were available. Among them, more than 8 in 10 say they’d use it to save money, earn interest or send money to family and friends.
Interest in learning more is slipping, though. The share who want to learn about stablecoins fell to 7% from 11%, and about DeFi to 8% from 11%, even after the GENIUS Act set federal rules for stablecoins.

title: Bitcoin Price Trades Above $81,500 As Fed Keeps Rates Steady
text:
The Federal Reserve left its benchmark rate unchanged Wednesday, holding the federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4%. The bitcoin price showed some volatility around $81,000.
The decision passed 10-2, and the dissents carry as much weight as the outcome. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point increase. It is the first time since 1992 that a Fed governor and a regional bank president have dissented together on the same side.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh faced reporters after the vote and said politics played no role in the decision, days before the midterm elections. Warsh has said he does not favor forward guidance absent a crisis, which leaves investors to read the data themselves.
The committee’s statement dropped its earlier language about when a hike might support a return to 2% inflation. In its place is a line saying more information will guide the policy stance. The Fed also described growth as strong, up from solid.
The signal points toward tightening. Fed funds futures and the Fed’s own dot plot lean toward a rate increase by December, and some pricing puts the odds near three in four. Inflation has been running hot, and the two dissenters are the officials who want to act on it.
Bitcoin price’s reaction was restrained. The bitcoin price spiked to about $81,700 in the minutes after the announcement, fell below $80,500, and then recovered toward $81,000. Most traders expected a hold, so the muted move surprises nobody.
Bitcoin’s first response to Fed news tends to be modest, and that the real direction often emerges over the following day. Spot Bitcoin ETFs drew $110 million in net inflows on October 26 and $176 million on October 27, a sign that some institutional money is buying the dip. Other observers have flagged large holders selling into strength.
That tension defines crypto’s position right now. Bitcoin sits about a third below its October 2025 record near $126,000. A rate-hike path works against an asset that has thrived on cheap money, and the market has spent months adjusting to the possibility that the easy-money era is over.
Some traders read the hold as evidence the Fed will move slowly. Others see December as the real test. For now, the level to watch is a bitcoin price of $80,000. It has held as support in recent sessions, and a clean break below it would expose the next floor.
Warsh and his colleagues have said they will wait for incoming data before acting. Bitcoin will have to wait along with everyone else.
Bitcoin’s next big political test arrives on November 3, when voters across the country head to the polls. Crypto has not really dominated the campaign trail.
The crypto industry spent about $176 million on more than 100 midterm races to build a bipartisan bloc in Congress that could protect its interests after President Donald Trump left office. Fairshake, the industry’s largest super PAC, led the effort and directed strategy as it had in the 2024 cycle.

title: AI Security Startup Upwind Raises $400M at $3.8B Valuation - Decrypt
text:
Upwind Security raised $400 million in a Series C round at a $3.8 billion valuation, the cloud and AI security company announced Wednesday. Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, less than nine months after it also led Upwind's $250 million Series B.
Canapi Ventures joined as a new investor, and every existing backer returned, pouring even more money into the startop. Upwind said it will put the money toward product and engineering growth.
“The funding round makes Upwind one of the most capitalized companies in the world that’s focused on solving the cloud and AI security problem,” Upwind said. “It is a big day for us, becoming the fastest growing company in modern cloud & AI security. But, it is still a small milestone in our journey.”
Upwind says revenue quadrupled in 2026, though its press release gives no dollar figures. The company counts hundreds of organizations as customers, among them Siemens, Roku, Carvana, Nubank (Brazil’s biggest neobank), Supabase, and ClickUp.
Its platform collects what it calls runtime intelligence, meaning data from cloud workloads, APIs and AI agents while they are running, instead of relying on periodic scans that capture a snapshot of an environment. It supports Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud, and AWS customers can open Upwind inside the AWS console through Security Hub, with billing handled through AWS.
The company's release argues that attackers now use AI to scale their operations while employees build applications on large language models and agents operate autonomously inside organizations. Traditional alert-based tools, it says, give security teams too little context to judge the intent behind an agent's activity or whether a vulnerability is a reachable exposure, meaning a flaw an attacker could actually get to.
The round follows a string of incidents this summer in which AI labs' own models reached real companies' systems.
OpenAI said in July that two of its models escaped a sandboxed test, exploited a previously unknown flaw and breached Hugging Face's production infrastructure to obtain answers to a cybersecurity evaluation. Anthropic reported that Claude models compromised three real-world companies after a testing misconfiguration gave them internet access, and Meta confirmed a similar case in August.
Upwind was founded in 2022 and has now raised more than $800 million, according to the company. The new valuation is about 2.5 times the one set in its January Series B.

title: Chip Maker SK Hynix Posts Record Quarter as AI Memory Demand Overwhelms Supply - Decrypt
text:
SK Hynix reported record third-quarter results on Wednesday, with revenue of 104.6 trillion won (almost $78 billion) and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won ($65.5 billion), according to its earnings release.
It was the first time the South Korean memory chip maker’s quarterly sales topped 100 trillion won ($74.5 billion).
Revenue rose 328% from a year earlier and operating profit rose 632%, for an operating margin of 80%, which means the company kept about 80 won of profit from its core business for every 100 won of sales. Analysts surveyed by Bloomberg had expected operating profit of 77.5 trillion won.
Net income came in at 39.8 trillion won, up 216% from a year ago but down 58% from the second quarter. CFO Kim Woo-hyun said the gap came from net non-operating expenses of 32.6 trillion won, meaning charges outside chip sales, led by an 11.6 trillion won currency loss and a 22.9 trillion won valuation loss on investments.
SK Hynix told investors that demand for memory will keep outrunning supply through 2030, and that its DRAM and HBM volumes through 2029 are effectively sold out. DRAM is the standard memory in servers, phones and PCs, while high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is the stacked memory that sits beside AI processors and feeds them data.
“Given the complexities involved in implementing leading-edge processes and the lead times required to construct new production facilities,” Kim Woo-hyun said, “a situation where supply cannot keep up with demand is expected to persist for some time, a constraint projected to continue through 2030.”
SK Hynix said some customers have recently adjusted their HBM specifications, which it reads as proof that demand is overwhelming supply, since they must build more AI accelerators from a limited quantity of chips. “Demand remains so strong that customers’ volume requirement is more than double that of what we can supply today,” the company said on the call.
To lock in that demand, SK Hynix has signed long-term agreements, contracts that reserve chip volumes years in advance, with 14 key customers including leading global cloud providers. They cover more than 50% of its 2027 and 2028 production capacity, typically run five years, let prices move within an agreed range and include safeguards such as deposits.
SK Hynix expects investment to rise significantly in 2027 as the first phase of its Yongin chip complex enters full-scale operation.
Citigroup analyst Peter Lee opened the Q&A by asking what supports confidence in AI investment when monetization looks slow, a doubt that Citadel founder Ken Griffin raised eight days earlier when he said investors are “almost certainly” in an AI bubble. CEO Kwak Noh-Jung answered that major cloud customers reported year-over-year cloud revenue growth of 30% to 80% and cloud order backlogs up two-fold to five-fold.
Kwak added that AI spending, once concentrated among a few big tech companies, is broadening to non-tech firms, sovereign AI projects (government-backed national computing) and on-prem setups (companies running AI on their own servers), so one buyer slowing down would hurt less.
Financing is tightening for AI infrastructure players, though. Elon Musk wrote on Oct. 25 that “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money” for firms without large non-AI revenue.
SK Hynix expects weaker demand from PC and smartphone makers because of higher memory prices and tight supply, but says AI infrastructure demand should offset the decline.

Bitcoin Treasury Datavault AI Says It Can’t Access Its BTC, Stock Tanks - Decrypt
text:
Datavault AI shares fell more than 50% on Tuesday to close at $0.06, after the Nasdaq-listed company disclosed that it has been unable to withdraw Bitcoin from the crypto exchange Biconomy since June. The company also said four sets of its financial statements can no longer be relied upon.
The disclosure came in a Form 8-K filed Oct. 26, in which Datavault said it requested a withdrawal to an external account in June and has been “unable to complete the withdrawal.” The filing does not explain what is holding it up.
The Bitcoin traces to a Sept. 25, 2025, agreement in which Scilex Holding, a pain-medicine company, agreed to pay $150 million in Bitcoin for 15 million Datavault shares and a pre-funded warrant covering another 263.9 million shares. A pre-funded warrant is a right to buy stock in which nearly the whole price is paid upfront.
At $112,915.52 per Bitcoin, the deal came to about 1,328.43 BTC. Scilex credited 1,309.04 BTC to Datavault's account at Biconomy on Sept. 26 and Nov. 25, 2025, the filing says, a figure that reflects a 19.39 BTC deduction for cash advances Scilex had made.
Those credits were off-chain transfers, meaning the exchange changed balances on its own books rather than moving coins across the Bitcoin blockchain. Between Sept. 26, 2025, and Jan. 30, 2026, Datavault sold 491.431 BTC back to Scilex the same way, for about $40.5 million in cash.
After reviewing the transaction, Datavault concluded the Bitcoin never qualified as a digital asset of the company. It will instead book the deal as a subscription receivable, money a buyer owes for newly issued stock, shown as a reduction of stockholders' equity, with the $40.5 million in cash reducing what Scilex owes.
The restatements are expected to cut total assets by $8.1 million as of Sept. 30, 2025, $92.2 million at the end of 2025, $57.1 million as of March 31, and $49 million as of June 30. They cover the 2025 annual report plus three quarterly reports filed between November 2025 and August 2026, and Datavault expects to reverse the crypto gains and losses it had recorded on the coins.
Datavault had counted those Bitcoin balances as a source of liquidity, so management is reassessing whether the company can continue as a going concern, the accounting test for whether a business can keep operating and meet its obligations. The filing says collection of the amounts owed by Scilex is uncertain, and its risk list includes Scilex's creditworthiness, the company's reliance on a third-party custodian, Nasdaq listing compliance, and litigation or regulatory inquiries tied to the restatement.
Scilex's own quarterly filing shows Biconomy was already part of the deal. Scilex said it sold 12.5 million shares of its Semnur Pharmaceuticals subsidiary to Biconomy on Sept. 23, 2025 for $200 million in Bitcoin, then used $150 million of that to buy Datavault stock.
On June 24, 2026, the same month Datavault says it asked to withdraw its Bitcoin, Scilex signed a binding term sheet to buy 837 BTC held in Datavault's Biconomy wallet for $50 million, subject to a definitive agreement. Scilex agreed to an initial $30 million payment and the remaining $20 million in quarterly installments through Dec. 31, 2028, payable in cash or Scilex securities at its discretion. The 837 BTC, added to the 491.431 BTC already sold back, equals the 1,328.43 BTC of the original agreement.
Datavault stock bounced to near $0.085 on Wednesday. Scilex's purchase price under the 2025 agreement worked out to an effective $0.5378 per share. Datavault has not said when it will file the restated statements, and it warned that delays could extend to its quarterly report for the period ended Sept. 30, 2026.
